passage: Thursday night. I dropped my science model in front of the whole class today, and the volcano split into three pieces. I did not cry. I went silent and said, "I am so stupid," to nobody. Arnab said it was only glue and cardboard, but I did not look at him. I hid in the library at lunch and sat there until the bell. When I told Mummy, she said, "Gopika, the model broke. You did not." I thought about that for a long time. Tomorrow Arnab and I will mend it with tape, if I can bring myself to show it. I am still a bit red in the face. 😔

qa.q: What happened to Gopika's science model?
qa.a: The volcano split into three pieces when Gopika dropped it.

qa.q: Why did Gopika say "I am so stupid" and hide in the library?
qa.a: She felt humiliated in front of the class, and the shame turned against herself, so she went silent. Her later thought about her mother's words suggests some of it is starting to ease.

qa.q: What did Gopika's mother say that separates the person from the act?
qa.a: She said, "The model broke. You did not." This tells Gopika the accident is not a verdict on her.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt when Gopika did not look at him?
qa.a: He probably felt puzzled or worried, since he was only trying to help by saying it was glue and cardboard.

grounding: A child humiliated by failure goes silent and calls herself stupid, and a parent separates the person from the act.

passage: At the village school's Annual Day, Saurabh froze on stage and could not remember his line. The hall went quiet. His face turned red, and he ran behind the big water pot at the back of the courtyard. Sonali ma'am found him with his knees pulled up. "I am stupid, ma'am," he whispered. She sat down on the ground next to him. "Forgetting a line is something that happened, not something you are," she said. "Do you want a minute?" He nodded. She told him about the time she forgot her own words at a wedding song. After a while Saurabh wiped his face and asked if he could watch the rest from beside her.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh run after he forgot his line?
qa.a: Saurabh ran behind the big water pot at the back of the courtyard.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's whisper "I am stupid, ma'am" tell us about his feelings?
qa.a: It tells us he was ashamed and turned the failure on himself. His red face and hiding suggest he wanted to disappear, though he still let her sit with him.

qa.q: What did Sonali ma'am do that made Saurabh feel safe?
qa.a: She sat next to him, separated the act from the person, gave him a minute and shared her own story of forgetting words.

qa.q: How might the audience have seen Saurabh's moment?
qa.a: Many probably felt kind and forgot it soon, though Saurabh may feel every eye was on him.

grounding: A child humiliated by failure hides and says he is stupid, and an adult separates the person from the act and offers safety.

passage:
Before. On Monday, Afreen borrowed Jagdish's ruler and snapped it in half by accident. She slid the pieces into her bag and would not meet his eyes when he asked if she had seen it.

During. On Tuesday, she began telling him long stories about where it could have gone, the corridor, the canteen, the bus. Jagdish looked confused, and Afreen's ears went hot.

After. On Wednesday, she stopped him at the gate and held out the two pieces. "I broke it. I am sorry. I can buy you a new one from my pocket money." Jagdish said it was only a ruler and thanked her for telling him. They walked in together.

qa.q: On which day did Afreen break the ruler?
qa.a: Afreen broke the ruler on Monday.

qa.q: Why did Afreen tell long stories about where the ruler could have gone?
qa.a: She was feeling guilty and was trying to explain around it without confessing. Her hot ears suggest how uncomfortable she was.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that repaired things?
qa.a: She confessed, said sorry and offered to buy a new ruler from her pocket money.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt when Afreen confessed?
qa.a: He was likely relieved and touched by her honesty, and he said it was only a ruler, so he did not want her to feel bad forever.

grounding: A child who broke something avoids eye contact, over-explains and finally confesses, with the repair kept in proportion, over three days.

passage: Beta, listen to what I did when I was nine. Our neighbour Madhuri's flowerpot was on the wall, and my ball knocked it down. It broke into pieces. I ran indoors and hid under the bed with my heart going like a drum. At dinner I would not look at my mother and I ate very little. Finally she asked, "Vandana, what is it?" I said, all in a rush, that I had done something, and she listened. The next morning I went across with my pocket money, said sorry to Madhuri, and helped her plant a new one. She thanked me and said it was only a pot. I felt lighter, and I did not carry it for years.

qa.q: What broke when Vandana's ball hit it?
qa.a: Madhuri's flowerpot broke when the ball knocked it off the wall.

qa.q: Why did Vandana hide under the bed and barely eat at dinner?
qa.a: She felt guilty about breaking the pot and was afraid of the consequences. Not meeting her mother's eyes shows she wanted to tell but was struggling.

qa.q: What made the repair feel proportionate?
qa.a: She said sorry, used her pocket money and helped plant a new pot, and Madhuri said it was only a pot, so she felt lighter.

qa.q: How might Vandana's mother have felt when she confessed?
qa.a: She was probably glad Vandana told the truth and wanted to help her put it right.

grounding: A child who broke something avoids eye contact and confesses; guilt about an action leads to repair and stays proportionate.

passage: "Please, Mummy, please, please, just till the end of the match," said Vandana, standing in the doorway in her pyjamas. Her eyes were wide and her voice was soft. Madhuri kept folding laundry. "It is a school night, Vandana." "Just half an hour. I will go to sleep straight away, I promise." Madhuri stopped and looked at her daughter. "I can hear how much you want it," she said. "And the answer is still no tonight. But I will record the last overs, and you can watch them after school." Vandana's lip wobbled, then she sighed. "Okay. Can I sit with you for five minutes?"

qa.q: What was Vandana doing when she asked her mother to watch the match?
qa.a: She was standing in the doorway in her pyjamas.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling as she said "please" over and over?
qa.a: She strongly wanted to watch the match and hoped her mother would give in. Her soft voice and wide eyes show she was trying to appeal to her mother's kindness.

qa.q: How did Madhuri hold a fair limit while hearing the need?
qa.a: She said she could hear how much Vandana wanted it, kept the school-night rule, and offered to record the last overs.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel saying no to her pleading child?
qa.a: She probably feels tender and a little torn, but firm that sleep matters on a school night.

grounding: A child pleads with please and a soft voice, and the adult hears the need while holding a fair limit.

passage: "Amma, please," said Pankaj. "Just one night at Arjun's house, I will be good." Uma did not look up from the tea she was pouring. "Which night?" "Saturday. Everyone is going." "Everyone?" "Well, five boys." He pressed his hands together. "Please, Amma. I will call you at nine, I will brush my teeth, please please." Uma set down the kettle and turned. "I hear you, Pankaj. I do not know Arjun's parents yet, so not this Saturday. But I will call them tomorrow, and we will see for next time." His shoulders dropped. "That is fair?" he asked, and she said it was.

qa.q: Which night did Pankaj want to spend at Arjun's house?
qa.a: Pankaj wanted to spend Saturday night at Arjun's house.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling as he pressed his hands together and said "please please"?
qa.a: He deeply wanted to go and was afraid of missing out with the other boys. His promises to call and brush his teeth show he wanted his mother to trust him.

qa.q: How did Uma respond fairly to his request?
qa.a: She said she heard him, explained she did not know Arjun's parents yet, refused this Saturday and promised to call them tomorrow.

qa.q: Why might Pankaj find the answer hard?
qa.a: He wanted to be with the five other boys, so waiting can feel like being left out, though his "That is fair?" suggests he begins to accept it.

grounding: A child begs with please for something wanted, and the adult hears the need while holding a fair limit.

passage: On the sports club's mud track, the race ended in a tangle when Ritu tripped over a root and skidded on her knees. She sat in the dirt, her lip trembling. Kalyani, who had been running behind, stopped and crouched next to her. She did not run on to the finish. "That looked painful," she said, and put a hand on Ritu's back. "Do you want to sit a bit?" Ritu nodded. Kalyani did not say it would stop hurting soon. She stayed until the coach arrived with the first-aid box. Ritu leaned on her arm all the way to the bench, and neither spoke.

qa.q: What did Ritu trip over?
qa.a: Ritu tripped over a root on the mud track.

qa.q: What did Kalyani's choice to stay put suggest about what she thought Ritu needed?
qa.a: She thought Ritu needed company and calm more than a promise, so she stayed close and asked if she wanted to sit. She could also have feared leaving a friend alone.

qa.q: Why was it wise that Kalyani did not say it would stop hurting soon?
qa.a: It avoids a promise she could not be sure of, and Ritu's need was for someone to stay with her.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt leaning on Kalyani's arm?
qa.a: She probably felt comforted and less alone, even though she said nothing.

grounding: A child stays close after a fall and reassures without empty promises, matching the friend's need.

passage: I was on the bench when Jatin dropped the ball in the last minute of our school cricket match. We lost by three runs. He stood in the field, staring at his hands. Amandeep, our captain, walked over slowly and stood next to him. He said, "It is okay," and then, "It happens." He did not say that we would definitely win next time. After a while he asked, "Want to walk back together?" Jatin nodded. I heard him say sorry, and Amandeep said he did not need to. I do not know if Jatin felt better, but his shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: By how many runs did the team lose?
qa.a: The team lost by three runs.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling as he stared at his hands?
qa.a: He was probably upset and blaming himself for the dropped ball. The observer cannot be sure, since he did not say much.

qa.q: What was helpful about what Amandeep did and said?
qa.a: He stayed close, said it was okay and that it happens, and offered to walk back together without an empty promise about next time.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt losing the match himself?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed too, but chose to support Jatin first.

grounding: A child stays close and reassures a friend after a mistake, matching the need and avoiding empty promises.

passage: Mahima, twelve, was helping her cousin Deepak with his homework on the veranda of their house in a small town. She read out the instructions for dividing a sack of wheat into equal bags. Deepak nodded and fidgeted with his pencil. When he wrote, the answer was wrong, and his eyes had a blank stare. "Do you follow?" asked Mahima. "Yes," he said, nodding again. She waited, then said, "Tell me the steps back, in your words." He opened his mouth and closed it. "I did not get the second part," he said quietly. She explained it again with dried beans as bags. This time he sorted them and grinned.

qa.q: What did Mahima read out the instructions for?
qa.a: She read out instructions for dividing a sack of wheat into equal bags.

qa.q: What might Deepak have been thinking when he kept nodding?
qa.a: He might have hoped to look as if he understood, or felt shy about admitting he was lost. His wrong answer and blank stare show the confusion.

qa.q: How did Mahima check whether Deepak really understood?
qa.a: She asked him to tell the steps back in his own words, which showed he missed the second part.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel when he finally says he did not get the second part?
qa.a: He might feel relieved that he could say it and was not laughed at, though he may also feel a little shy.

grounding: A child hides confusion by nodding and giving wrong answers, and asking him to explain back checks understanding.

passage: In an art class in Milan, the teacher explained in English how to mix a green using blue and yellow. Valentina, who had only learned English for a year, nodded at every sentence. She fidgeted with her brush and stared at the palette. When she started, she mixed red and yellow by mistake. Mei, at the next table, noticed and leaned over. "Do you want me to say it slowly?" The teacher came over and asked Valentina to tell her back what she would do next. Valentina pointed at the blue pot and said, "I need this?" The teacher smiled and repeated it, one step at a time.

qa.q: Which two colours did Valentina mix by mistake?
qa.a: Valentina mixed red and yellow by mistake.

qa.q: What was Valentina probably feeling when she nodded at every sentence?
qa.a: She probably felt unsure and did not want to be the one who did not understand. Her fidgeting and mistake suggest she was confused, though nodding may also have been polite.

qa.q: How did the teacher check what Valentina understood?
qa.a: She asked Valentina to say back what she would do next, and then repeated the instructions one step at a time.

qa.q: How might Mei have seen Valentina's confusion?
qa.a: She noticed the mix-up and offered to slow down, so she likely thought Valentina needed help and not that she was careless.

grounding: A child hides confusion by nodding, and asking her to explain back checks understanding, here in a second language.

passage: Note on Class 4, science period. Uma announced that whales drink sea water to stay alive, and the class nodded. Pankaj tilted his head and said, "Really? How do you know?" Uma said she had heard it from her cousin. Pankaj did not argue but asked if we could look it up. I brought out two library books, and the children looked through the index together. They found a page saying that whales get water from their food. Uma looked surprised. Pankaj said, "Good that we checked." I praised him for asking and Uma for changing her mind. I will ask the class next week where our facts come from.

qa.q: What did Uma announce about whales?
qa.a: Uma announced that whales drink sea water to stay alive.

qa.q: What was Pankaj probably thinking when he said "Really? How do you know?"
qa.a: He was doubtful and wanted a reason before believing it. He did not argue, so he may also have been simply curious.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to build healthy skepticism?
qa.a: She brought library books so the children could check together, and praised both Pankaj's question and Uma's willingness to change her mind.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt when the book disagreed with her cousin?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and perhaps a little embarrassed, but she was willing to accept the evidence.

grounding: A child questions a claim with 'really' and 'how do you know', and checks a source.

passage: Saturday. Charu told everyone at lunch that you can see the Great Wall from space with your bare eyes. Everyone said "Wow". Charu turned to me and asked, "Rekha, why the face?" I said, "Really? Who says?" She said her brother. I did not say it was wrong, I just wanted to know how he knew. After school I went to the library and asked the librarian. She showed me an atlas and a book on space. It says the wall is very long but very thin, so it is hard to see. I told Charu at the gate. She frowned, then laughed and said she would ask her brother where he got it. 🤔

qa.q: What did Charu say you can see from space?
qa.a: Charu said you can see the Great Wall from space with your bare eyes.

qa.q: Why did Rekha say "Really? Who says?"
qa.a: She was not sure the claim was true and wanted to know where it came from. She was not trying to be rude, only curious about how Charu's brother knew.

qa.q: What helped Rekha check the claim?
qa.a: She went to the library, asked the librarian and looked in an atlas and a book on space.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when Rekha told her at the gate?
qa.a: She was probably a bit surprised and possibly embarrassed, but she laughed and wanted to check with her brother, so she stayed open.

grounding: A child says 'really' and 'who says' to a claim that sounds off, and learns to check sources.

passage: Hemant's grandson had asked why the teacher never hurries anyone, so Hemant told him a story. "When I was ten, my classmate Omkar was the quietest boy in the room. When the teacher asked a question, Omkar looked out of the window and tapped his chin. The rest of us shouted answers. Our teacher would raise her hand and say, 'Wait.' She waited, and waited. Five, six seconds felt like forever. Then Omkar would say the best answer of all. I learned from her that silence is often thinking. Now I wait for you, too." The boy grinned and looked out of the window, tapping his chin.

qa.q: What did Omkar do when the teacher asked a question?
qa.a: Omkar looked out of the window and tapped his chin.

qa.q: What does Hemant believe was going on in Omkar's mind during those quiet seconds?
qa.a: He believes Omkar was thinking, not failing to know, since the best answer came after the wait. It is his reading, though, and the story does not say what Omkar was thinking.

qa.q: What could a teacher do for a child who goes quiet before answering?
qa.a: Raise a hand, ask the class to wait, and give the child a few extra seconds, as this teacher did.

qa.q: How might the other children have felt waiting for Omkar?
qa.a: They may have felt impatient at first since waiting seemed to last forever, but they learned that his answers were worth it.

grounding: A child goes quiet and taps his chin while working out an answer; waiting a few extra seconds lets the child finish.

passage: The quiz bell was about to ring, and the hall was loud with chairs scraping. Sonali ma'am asked the last question, and Mehak, at the back, went quiet and looked away toward the window. Her fingers tapped her chin. Others started calling out guesses, and a boy said, "She does not know." Sonali ma'am held up her hand. "Wait a moment." The clock kept ticking, and the noise slowly settled. Then Mehak turned and said, softly, "It is the second river, because the first one is a tributary." The teacher smiled and said that was right. Mehak looked down and hid her grin.

qa.q: Where was Mehak sitting during the quiz?
qa.a: Mehak was sitting at the back of the hall.

qa.q: What did Mehak's tapping of her chin and looking toward the window suggest?
qa.a: It suggested she was thinking through the answer. The boy thought she did not know, which is another reading, but her answer showed it was thinking.

qa.q: What could Sonali ma'am do when others rush to call out an answer?
qa.a: Hold up her hand and let the room settle, giving the thinker a few extra seconds.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt with others guessing around her?
qa.a: She may have felt pressured and rushed, and relieved when the teacher asked everyone to wait.

grounding: A child goes quiet and taps her chin while working out an answer, and waiting lets her finish, with quiz-time pressure.

passage: I have watched Dolma every day from my window, since her school is right across the road. Today was her first day in the new class, and her father Anirban walked her to the gate. She stopped a few steps before it. She held her strap with both hands and looked at the other children running in. Anirban crouched and pointed at the classroom, and I could not hear what he said. She stayed there for nearly a minute. Then she took one step, stopped, and took another. At the door a girl waved, and Dolma waved a little. I could not tell if she was scared or just being careful.

qa.q: Who walked Dolma to the gate?
qa.a: Her father Anirban walked her to the gate.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been feeling when she stopped before the gate?
qa.a: She was probably nervous about the new class and wanted a pause before going in. The observer cannot tell if she was scared or just being careful.

qa.q: How could Anirban help Dolma with a new class?
qa.a: Preview the classroom with her, walk in with her if she wants and let her take the steps at her own pace.

qa.q: How might the girl who waved at the door have seen Dolma?
qa.a: She probably saw a new child who needed a friendly sign, and her wave was welcoming.

grounding: A child hangs back before a new class; apprehension is a cautious pause and eases with a supportive adult.

passage:
Before. On Monday, before the inter-school match, Farhan sat on the bench and could not stop tapping his foot. Coach Naveen noticed that he had not touched his water.

During. On Wednesday, the coach took the team to the ground where they would play. Farhan walked the boundary and stood at his batting spot. Naveen asked him to play three practice balls, and Farhan's grip slowly loosened.

After. On Saturday, Farhan still felt his stomach flutter at the gate, but he told Naveen, "I know where I stand." He took a breath, walked in and hit his first ball. Afterwards he said the pause at the gate was just his body getting ready.

qa.q: Which day did the coach take the team to the ground?
qa.a: The coach took the team to the ground on Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Farhan mean when he said the pause at the gate was just his body getting ready?
qa.a: He understood his nerves as a cautious pause and not a sign he could not do it. The earlier practice made the pause easier.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that eased Farhan's apprehension?
qa.a: He took the team to preview the ground and asked Farhan to play three practice balls.

qa.q: How might Naveen have seen Farhan's tapping foot on Monday?
qa.a: He probably read it as nerves before a big day and made a note to help him prepare.

grounding: A child hangs back before a match; apprehension eases with preview, practice and a supportive adult, over separate days.

passage: My cousin Kamal lost his school ID card on the way to the exam hall, and the guard would not let him in. He searched his bag three times. His face went grey and his hands shook. Rukmini, his class teacher, found it in the corridor, under a bench, and held it up from across the hall. Kamal stared at it. Then his breath came out in a long whoosh, his shoulders dropped, and he sat down on the step and laughed, though his eyes were wet. He looked tired all of a sudden, as if he had run a long way. I cannot say if he was happy or just worn out.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini find the ID card?
qa.a: Rukmini found the ID card in the corridor, under a bench.

qa.q: What did Kamal's long exhale and sagging shoulders suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest relief after tension. His wet eyes and laughter fit that, though the observer notes he might simply be worn out.

qa.q: How could a teacher or relative help Kamal after such a scare?
qa.a: Let him sit for a moment to settle, offer water and remind him he is in time, before he goes into the hall.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel holding up the card?
qa.a: She probably feels glad and relieved she could help, since she held it up from across the hall.

grounding: A child exhales, slumps and laughs after a lost item is found, and the drop may look like tiredness.

passage:
Before. On Monday morning, Noor's hands were cold before the maths test, and she kept asking Thomas whether he thought it would be hard. He said he did not know.

During. On Tuesday, the teacher handed back the papers in the assembly hall. Noor gripped the edge of her desk, and when her paper came, she turned it over slowly. She got a good mark. She let out a huge breath and put her head on her arms.

After. On Wednesday she was late to school and yawned all through the morning. She told Thomas she felt like a wrung-out cloth. He laughed and shared his water.

qa.q: On which day did Noor get her paper back?
qa.a: Noor got her paper back on Tuesday.

qa.q: Why did Noor put her head on her arms after seeing her mark?
qa.a: She felt relief after being tense for a day, and the physical drop can look like tiredness. She could also have been overwhelmed after the worry.

qa.q: What does Noor's yawning on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests that relief after tension can leave a child worn out, as she said she felt like a wrung-out cloth.

qa.q: How might Thomas have seen Noor's questions before the test?
qa.a: He probably understood she was nervous, and said he did not know instead of promising it would be easy.

grounding: A child slumps and looks tired after relief from a scary test, over separate days.

passage:
Before. On Monday night, Joseph asked his mother Reena, "What if I forget everything tomorrow? What if the paper is too hard?" He rubbed his stomach and said it hurt.

During. On Tuesday morning, he could not sit still and left his breakfast half-eaten. Reena sat down and asked him to say the three topics he was most worried about. They wrote them on a card and went through each one for five minutes.

After. On Wednesday, Joseph said the stomach ache had gone after he tucked the card in his pocket. He still felt nervous, but he said, "I have a plan now."

qa.q: What did Joseph ask his mother on Monday night?
qa.a: Joseph asked, "What if I forget everything tomorrow? What if the paper is too hard?"

qa.q: What did Joseph's stomach ache and what if questions show about his state?
qa.a: They show he was worried, and the worry showed up in his body. It could also be partly hunger or tiredness, though the plan helped.

qa.q: What simple plan did Reena help him make?
qa.a: She asked him to name the three topics he was most worried about, wrote them on a card and went through each one.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt seeing Joseph leave his breakfast half-eaten?
qa.a: She was probably concerned for him and wanted to help him make the worry smaller.

grounding: A school-age child asks what if questions and has a stomach ache before a test; listening and a simple plan help.

passage: Minakshi's granddaughter had been fretting about a school trip, and Minakshi sat beside her on the swing. "When I was ten, Bhavna and I were to go on our first school trip, and I could not sleep. What if I get lost? What if the bus breaks? My tummy ached the whole night. My mother did not tell me not to worry. She said, 'Let's make a plan,' and we wrote: stay with Bhavna, keep the teacher's number, carry water. I put that in my pocket. Next day the ache was smaller." The girl said quietly, "What is my plan, then?"

qa.q: What did Minakshi and her mother write in the plan?
qa.a: They wrote: stay with Bhavna, keep the teacher's number, carry water.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi's tummy ache the night before the trip?
qa.a: She was worried about getting lost or the bus breaking down, and the worry showed in her body. Not sleeping shows how strongly she felt it.

qa.q: What did Minakshi's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She did not tell her not to worry, but made a simple plan with her and let her keep it in her pocket.

qa.q: How might the granddaughter feel when she asks "What is my plan, then?"
qa.a: She probably feels a bit hopeful and reassured that a worry can be turned into steps.

grounding: A school-age child asks what if questions and has a stomach ache; listening and a simple plan help.
